steps.body: The pattern earns its keep in the wild: rows of chairs, packs of stickers, cents in dimes. The workflow uses everything you own: **spot the tens unit → run the small fact → read in units → guard with an estimate**. This lesson is the whole course, one story at a time.
First move: which way is the story pointing?

widget.prompt: Sort each story by the operation it needs.

items.label: 4 packs of 20 stickers — how many stickers?
items.feedback: The total is the mystery, built from 4 equal groups of 2 tens: 4 × 20 = 80.

items.label: 80 stickers shared equally into 4 albums
items.feedback: The total (80) is known and gets split — 80 ÷ 4 = 20 per album.

items.label: 4 shelves with 20 books on each
items.feedback: Equal groups building an unknown total: 4 × 2 tens = 8 tens = 80 books.

items.label: 80 chairs set out in 4 equal rows
items.feedback: The 80 is given and gets split into rows: 80 ÷ 4 = 20 chairs per row.

widget.missFeedback: Find each story's total: unknown and being built → ×; known and being split → ÷. (The word-problem compass still works with tens.)
widget.successFeedback: Same numbers, opposite directions — the compass from the multiplication course points true with tens aboard.

predict.prompt: '4 shelves with 20 books each — how many books in all?' Which operation builds the answer?
predict.reveal: Groups given, total wanted: multiply. Total given, shares wanted: divide. Sort stories by what's MISSING, not by their keywords — 'each' shows up in both kinds.

explanationVariants: Each dime is 1 ten of cents, so 7 dimes are 7 tens: 70 cents.
Run the workflow: unit is tens (of cents), fact is 7 × 1, read in tens: 70.

widget.prompt: A dime is worth 10 cents. How many cents are 7 dimes worth?

commonErrors.feedback: 17 adds 7 + 10. Each of the 7 coins is worth a whole ten — seven tens multiply up to 70.
710 glues 7 and 10 side by side. The 7 counts tens: seven tens read as 70.
7 counts the COINS. Their value is in tens of cents — read those 7 tens as 70.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 7 coins × 1 ten each = 7 tens of cents.

steps.body: Two-step stories still follow the workshop rules: find the first pile, **say it out loud**, then let the second step act on the right pile. And the ch3 habit stands guard over the final answer — round, compute friendly, compare.
A one-step warmup at full size.
explanationVariants: 6 rows of 3 tens: 6 × 3 = 18, read in tens: 180 chairs.
Guard: 6 × 30 is a bit under 6 × 40 = 240 and well over 6 × 20 = 120 — 180 sits comfortably between.

widget.prompt: Chairs come in rows of 30. The hall needs 6 full rows. How many chairs is that?

commonErrors.feedback: 18 is the tens count — eighteen TENS of chairs. The badge writes it as 180.
36 adds 6 + 30. Six whole rows of 30 multiply: run 6 × 3 in tens.
1800 wears an extra badge — only one ten is in play (30's). Eighteen tens are 180.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 6 × 3 tens = 18 tens. Read it back as a number.

steps.body: Chain a whole plan — build, then change the pile.

widget.prompt: 3 boxes hold 40 crayons each; then 20 crayons are given away. Build the whole plan as one expression.

commonBuilds.feedback: Given-away crayons LEAVE the pile — the chain's second link subtracts.
3 + 40 joins the box count to one box's crayons. The boxes are equal groups — step one multiplies them.

widget.missFeedback: Build the pile first (3 boxes × 40), then remove the 20 given away.
widget.successFeedback: 3 × 40 − 20 = 120 − 20 = 100 crayons kept. Build, then change — the workshop chain with tens aboard.

explanationVariants: 6 × 20 is 12 tens = 120 — Jo's 80 is four-tickets money (4 × 20), not six.
Even 5 tickets cost 100; six must cost more. An 80 can't survive the size check.

widget.prompt: Tickets cost $20 each. Jo says 6 tickets cost $80 total. What does one glance tell you?

options.label: Busted — six 20s make 12 tens, which is $120, not $80
options.feedback: The tens count does it in one glance: 6 × 2 tens = 12 tens = 120. Jo priced only four tickets.

options.label: Fine — 80 is a reasonably big number
options.feedback: Big compared to what? Five tickets alone cost $100 — six can't cost less. Size checks compare, never just admire.

options.label: You can't tell without a calculator
options.feedback: The small fact 6 × 2 (in tens) settles it in your head: 12 tens is 120, and 80 falls short.

options.label: Busted — tickets never cost $20
options.feedback: Ticket trivia isn't math. The bust comes from the numbers: 6 × 20 must reach 120.

steps.body: The course capstone: total, change, guard.
hints: Total first: 7 packs of 9 tens of pencils.
The art room takes 130: subtract, and guard the answer (≈ 630 − 100).
explanationVariants: Total: 7 × 90 = 630. After the gift: 630 − 130 = 500. Guard: ≈ 600 − 100 = 500 — dead on.
Unit route: 63 tens minus 13 tens = 50 tens = 500 pencils remain.

widget.prompt: A school buys 7 packs of 90 pencils, then gives 130 pencils to the art room. How many pencils does the school keep?

commonErrors.feedback: 630 is the full purchase — step one done! The art room's 130 leave the pile. Subtract them.
760 ADDED the gift. Pencils that go to the art room leave the school's pile — the second step subtracts.
50 is the answer in TENS (63 tens − 13 tens) — read the badge: fifty tens are 500 pencils.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two steps: total the packs (7 × 9 tens), then subtract 130 — or work it all in tens: 63 − 13.

steps.body: That's the whole course, working as one machine.
takeaways: Spot the tens unit, run the small fact, read the badge.
Two-step stories: build the pile, say it out loud, then change it.
The guard checks every final answer — the habit that never retires.
steps.teaser: a brand-new course begins: Fractions from Scratch — what happens when we cut things into equal parts.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Translate the story into tens BEFORE computing: "5 bags of 30" becomes 5 × 3 tens. Run the small fact (15), read the badge (150). Story → tens → fact → badge, every time.

explanationVariants: 2 rows of 5 tens: 2 × 5 = 10, read in tens: 100 chairs.
Ten tens trade up into exactly one hundred — the chapter-1 trade, closing the loop.

widget.prompt: 2 rows of 50 chairs — how many chairs?

options.feedback: 2 × 5 tens = 10 tens = 100 — ten tens trade up into one hundred.
10 is the tens count. Ten TENS of chairs read as 100.
52 adds 2 + 50. Two whole rows of 50 multiply: 2 × 5 in tens.
